  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Comparing covariance structures}

`lmm_animal()` offers five multivariate covariance structures:

1. unstructured `G`, unstructured `E` (the default);
2. unstructured `G`, diagonal `E`;
3. factor `G`, unstructured `E`;
4. factor `G`, diagonal `E`;
5. factor `G`, shared-factor `E`: the same latent factors drive `G` and `E`.

This vignette simulates five traits from a two-factor `G` and a diagonal `E`
(so model 4 is the true one) and fits all five. It scores each fit twice: by
its error against the simulated truth, which only a simulation can give, and by
held-out predictive density with `fit_loo()`, which is the question a user can
ask of real data.


``` r
library(stanimal)
```

## Simulation

The first factor loads on traits 1 to 3, the second on traits 3 to 5.


``` r
set.seed(1234)
n_traits <- 5L
n_factors <- 2L
traits <- paste0("t", seq_len(n_traits))

Lambda <- matrix(c(0.90,  0.00,
                   0.85,  0.00,
                   0.70,  0.30,
                   0.00,  0.80,
                   0.00, -0.70), n_traits, n_factors, byrow = TRUE)
Psi <- c(0.35, 0.40, 0.30, 0.45, 0.50)
G <- Lambda %*% t(Lambda) + diag(Psi)
E <- diag(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95))
dimnames(G) <- dimnames(E) <- list(traits, traits)

n_gen <- 5; n_breed <- 100
ped <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n_gen * n_breed),
                  sire = NA_integer_, dam = NA_integer_,
                  sex = NA_character_)
ped$sex[seq_len(n_breed)] <- sample(rep(c("M", "F"), each = n_breed / 2))
for (g in 2:n_gen) {
  kids <- ((g - 1) * n_breed + 1):(g * n_breed)
  pool <- ped[ped$id < min(kids), ]
  ped$sire[kids] <- sample(pool$id[pool$sex == "M"], n_breed, TRUE)
  ped$dam[kids]  <- sample(pool$id[pool$sex == "F"], n_breed, TRUE)
  ped$sex[kids]  <- sample(c("M", "F"), n_breed, TRUE)
}
A <- makeA(ped)

n <- nrow(A)
X <- cbind(Intercept = 1, sex = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
           age = round(rnorm(n, 3, 0.5), 2))
B <- rbind(rep(10, n_traits), rep(1.5, n_traits), rep(0.4, n_traits))
Y <- X %*% B +
  t(chol(A)) %*% matrix(rnorm(n * n_traits), n) %*% chol(G) +
  matrix(rnorm(n * n_traits), n) %*% chol(E)
colnames(Y) <- traits
```

## Fitting the five structures

Every fit uses the same chain settings, the unstructured parts the same LKJ
prior and the factor parts the same horseshoe, so differences reflect the
structure. `A` is decomposed once and passed to every fit as `eigen_A`.


``` r
e <- eigen(A, symmetric = TRUE)
eigen_A <- list(Q = e$vectors, lambda = e$values)

fit_one <- function(...) {
  elapsed <- system.time(
    fit <- lmm_animal(Y, X, A, eigen_A = eigen_A,
                      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
                      refresh = 0, seed = 1, ...))[["elapsed"]]
  attr(fit, "elapsed") <- elapsed
  fit
}
factor_args <- list(genetic_structure = "factor", n_factors = n_factors,
                    hs_global_scale = 2, hs_slab_scale = 2)

fits <- list(
  "G us, E us"         = fit_one(),
  "G us, E diag"       = fit_one(residual_structure = "diagonal"),
  "G factor, E us"     = do.call(fit_one, factor_args),
  "G factor, E diag"   = do.call(fit_one, c(factor_args,
                                            residual_structure = "diagonal")),
  "G factor, E shared" = do.call(fit_one, c(factor_args,
                                            residual_structure = "shared_factor"))
)
```

## Against the truth

Relative MSE divides each elementwise mean squared error by the mean squared
truth, so errors on quantities with different scales can be compared. The
correlation comparison uses the upper triangle, since the diagonal is always 1.
`min_ess` is the smallest bulk effective sample size across the unique elements
of `G`.


``` r
relative_mse <- function(estimate, truth)
  mean((estimate - truth)^2) / mean(truth^2)
upper <- function(S) cov2cor(S)[upper.tri(S)]

score <- function(fit) {
  G_hat <- draws_mean(fit, "G")
  E_hat <- draws_mean(fit, "E")
  G_draws <- fit_draws(fit)$G
  keep <- which(lower.tri(G), arr.ind = TRUE)
  keep <- rbind(keep, cbind(seq_len(n_traits), seq_len(n_traits)))
  ess <- apply(keep, 1, function(ij)
    posterior::ess_bulk(G_draws[ij[1], ij[2], ]))
  c(G = relative_mse(G_hat, G),
    E = relative_mse(E_hat, E),
    h2 = relative_mse(diag(G_hat) / diag(G_hat + E_hat),
                      diag(G) / diag(G + E)),
    corrG = relative_mse(upper(G_hat), upper(G)),
    min_ess = min(ess),
    divergences = sum(fit$diagnostic_summary(quiet = TRUE)$num_divergent),
    time_s = attr(fit, "elapsed"))
}
round(t(sapply(fits, score)), 3)
#>                        G     E    h2 corrG  min_ess divergences  time_s
#> G us, E us         0.038 0.037 0.010 0.069 2679.637           0  21.967
#> G us, E diag       0.029 0.011 0.006 0.052 3872.619           0  14.850
#> G factor, E us     0.043 0.040 0.010 0.072 1790.653           0  35.924
#> G factor, E diag   0.027 0.009 0.005 0.050 2154.065           0  31.207
#> G factor, E shared 0.026 0.019 0.006 0.050 2859.964           0 138.000
```

## Held-out predictive density

`fit_loo()` leaves out one individual at a time. Relatives share breeding values,
so the term for an animal is the density of its traits given every other animal,
computed after the fit from the draws (non-factorized LOO). Every fit is to the
same response, so the constant the standardization contributes cancels in the
comparison.


``` r
loos <- lapply(fits, fit_loo, eigen_A = eigen_A)
sapply(loos, function(l) sum(l$diagnostics$pareto_k > 0.7))
#>         G us, E us       G us, E diag     G factor, E us   G factor, E diag 
#>                  0                  0                  0                  0 
#> G factor, E shared 
#>                  0
loo::loo_compare(loos)
#>               model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse       diag_diff diag_elpd
#>    G factor, E diag       0.0     0.0      NA                          
#>        G us, E diag      -1.1     0.9    0.89 |elpd_diff| < 4          
#>  G factor, E shared      -4.1     1.5    1.00                          
#>      G factor, E us     -10.7     3.2    1.00                          
#>          G us, E us     -12.0     3.1    1.00
#> 
#> Diagnostic flags present.
#> See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
#> or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.
```

Every model is compared with the best one: `elpd_diff` is its loss relative to
that model and `se_diff` the standard error of the difference. A difference
smaller than about twice its standard error is not an ordering.

Here the ranking separates the residual structure clearly. Both
unstructured-`E` models lose more than three standard errors against the best
fit, so the data prefer a diagonal `E`, which is what generated them. The
shared-factor model sits between the two: it forces the factors that drive `G`
to drive `E` too, which a diagonal `E` does not have. The genetic structure is
not separated: with a diagonal `E`, the factor and unstructured `G` are about one
standard error apart. That matches the table against the truth, where those two
fits have nearly the same error. With five traits a factor `G` saves few
parameters; its advantage, in accuracy and in sampling time, grows with the
number of traits, where an unstructured `G` becomes expensive.

Timings are single runs of the `lmm_animal()` call. The shared-factor model is
the slowest to sample.
